analysis.one_liner: Cuts capital gains tax rates in half, speeds up depreciation for high-tech equipment, and adds a minimum tax on foreign-owned corporations.
analysis.headline: A Republican-sponsored tax bill that halved capital gains rates and taxed foreign-owned corporations died in committee in September 1992 without ever getting a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut the top individual capital gains rate from 28% to 15% and the corporate capital gains rate to 15% [S3]. It would have let companies write off semiconductor manufacturing and advanced-technology equipment over just three years instead of five, reducing their tax bills [S2][S3]. To partially pay for this, it would have imposed a new minimum tax on foreign corporations doing business in the U.S. and domestic corporations at least one-quarter foreign-owned [S2][S3]. It was introduced late in the 102nd Congress, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never received a hearing or vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who realize capital gains — overwhelmingly higher-income households and corporations, since capital gains flow disproportionately to the top of the income scale — would pay a top rate of 15% instead of 28% [S3]. Semiconductor, advanced materials, and advanced technology manufacturers would get faster depreciation deductions, lowering taxes on new equipment purchases [S2][S3]. Domestic corporations would also benefit competitively from the new tax on their foreign-owned rivals [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Sets a maximum 15% individual capital gains rate, down from the prior 28% top rate, and cuts the corporate capital gains rate to 15% as well [S3].

Allows a three-year depreciable life for semiconductor manufacturing equipment and equipment used to make advanced materials or develop advanced technologies, letting companies deduct the cost of equipment much faster than the standard five-year schedule [S2][S3].

Imposes a minimum tax on domestic corporations that are 25%-or-more foreign-owned and on foreign corporations doing business in the United States, roughly 1.7% of gross receipts from manufactured products, designed to ensure such companies pay at least some U.S. tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would lose substantial revenue from the capital gains cuts and accelerated depreciation, a burden ultimately spread across other taxpayers or future borrowing [S3]. Foreign and foreign-owned corporations manufacturing in the U.S. would owe the new minimum tax [S2][S3]. Because capital gains accrue mostly to the wealthiest households, the rate cut's benefits would be heavily concentrated at the top.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the top capital gains rate from 28% to 15% primarily benefits the households and corporations that realize gains, which skews heavily toward the wealthiest taxpayers, and would reduce federal revenue [S3].

The new minimum tax on foreign-owned corporations could discourage foreign companies from building or operating manufacturing facilities in the United States, an objection its supporters would have had to weigh against the revenue it raises [S3].
Accelerated depreciation is a targeted tax break for a specific set of industries, favoring them over other businesses that buy equipment with no such preference [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs large tax reductions for investors and high-tech manufacturers with a narrower tax increase on foreign-owned corporations. The capital gains cut, worth roughly half the prior top rate, would flow overwhelmingly to wealthier taxpayers and reduce federal revenue, while the provisions for ordinary working people are indirect at best — none of the bill's text is aimed at wages, benefits, or consumer costs. The foreign-corporation minimum tax is the only provision that raises money rather than giving it away, but it offsets only part of the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 10, 1992, sent to the Ways and Means Committee, and the committee never took it up before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Duncan Hunter (R-CA) introduced the bill on September 10, 1992 [S1][S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
Nine Republican representatives signed on as cosponsors; no further action was recorded before the Congress ended [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the federal Treasury kept the higher 28% capital gains rate and foreign-owned corporations avoided the new minimum tax; wealthy investors and tech manufacturers gained nothing from the proposal's failure to move.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all nine cosponsors were Republicans, and no floor votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape beyond sponsorship cannot be measured.

industries.note: The bill gives these manufacturers a three-year write-off for equipment instead of five, a direct tax subsidy [S2][S3]. The cost lands on the Treasury and other taxpayers, while no consumer benefit is specified in the bill.

The top capital gains rate would drop from 28% to 15%, roughly halving the tax on realized gains [S3]. Gains concentrate among the wealthiest taxpayers, so the benefit runs against the broader taxpayer base that would backfill the lost revenue.

industries.industry: Foreign and foreign-owned corporations operating in the U.S.
industries.note: These companies would owe a new minimum tax of about 1.7% of gross receipts from manufactured products [S3]. The provision raises revenue but targets a specific class of firms, potentially deterring foreign manufacturing investment.
